title: Linear Approximation and Differentials
short: Near a, f(x) ≈ f(a) + f′(a)(x − a).

blocks.html: Near the point of tangency a curve and its tangent line are almost the same. That makes the tangent line a cheap way to estimate values that are hard to compute. With the The Chain Rule we can do this for almost any function.

The linearization of $f$ at $a$ is $\role[linear estimate]{output}{L(x)} = \role[height at a]{output}{f(a)} + \role[slope at a]{rate}{f'(a)}\role[distance from a]{input}{(x - a)}$, and $f(x) \approx L(x)$ for $x$ near $a$. In differential form: if $x$ changes by $dx$, then $f$ changes by about $dy = f'(x)\,dx$.

opts.task: Zoom in around $(25, 5)$ until you cannot tell the curve from the line.

blocks.html: The derivative is the limit of $\frac{f(x) - f(a)}{x - a}$, so for $x$ near $a$ the quotient is close to $f'(a)$: $f(x) - f(a) \approx f'(a)(x - a)$. Rearranged, that is $f(x) \approx f(a) + f'(a)(x - a)$. The error shrinks faster than $x - a$ itself, which is what "the curve looks straight up close" means. The farther $x$ is from $a$, the worse the estimate.

blocks.title: A square root
steps: The true value is $5.0990\ldots$: off by about $0.001$.

blocks.title: Measurement error
blocks.q: A disk's radius is measured as 10 cm with a possible error of 0.1 cm. Estimate the possible error in its area.

blocks.html: Using a base point that is far away, or one where the values are not easy. The method only helps if $f(a)$ and $f'(a)$ are known exactly and $x$ is close to $a$. Check: also note which side the error lies on. For $\sqrt{x}$, which bends downward, the tangent line lies above the curve, so $L$ overestimates.
Physicists use these approximations constantly: $\sin x \approx x$ and $(1 + x)^n \approx 1 + nx$ for small $x$ are both linearizations at 0.
